one_liner: Being very sleepy during the day despite sleeping at least seven hours, for months, with no other cause found.
in_simple_words: Hypersomnolence disorder is more than feeling tired. A person sleeps a full night, often longer, and still fights to stay awake by day, falls asleep unintentionally, takes long naps that don't refresh, or struggles to wake up at all ('sleep drunkenness'). It goes on for three months or more and isn't explained by poor sleep, apnoea, medication, or another condition. It's often dismissed as laziness. It's a real neurological condition, and there is treatment.
what_it_can_feel_like: I slept ten hours and still couldn't keep my eyes open in meetings. People thought I was bored.
Waking up felt like climbing out of wet concrete, every single day.
The sleep study was the first time anyone believed me.
common_signs: Sleeping seven hours or more and still very sleepy by day
Falling asleep unintentionally, or long naps that don't refresh
Great difficulty waking, feeling confused or clumsy for a while after
At least three times a week for three months or more
Daytime life affected: work, driving, relationships
No other explanation, like apnoea, medication, or not enough sleep

myths_vs_facts.myth: Sleeping a lot means you're lazy or depressed.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Hypersomnolence is a neurological disorder. Depression can cause oversleeping too, which is why a proper assessment matters.
People with hypersomnolence already sleep plenty. More sleep doesn't help; treatment does.
They're related but different. Narcolepsy has sudden sleep attacks and often cataplexy; hypersomnolence is constant sleepiness and long sleep.

how_common.plain: Hypersomnolence disorder is uncommon in the general population but makes up a meaningful share of people seen in sleep clinics.
how_common.figure: DSM-5-TR text: about 1% of the general population report sleep drunkenness; around 5–10% of sleep-clinic patients with daytime sleepiness are diagnosed with hypersomnolence disorder
how_common.note: Figures from the DSM-5-TR text; need primary sources.

what_helps.plain_summary: Diagnosis needs a sleep study to rule out apnoea and narcolepsy. Treatment usually combines wake-promoting medication, prescribed and monitored by a sleep specialist, with planned naps and a regular schedule. Treating any depression or other conditions helps. Driving safety is discussed as part of care.
evidence_based_options: Wake-promoting medication, prescribed and monitored by a sleep specialist
Scheduled naps and a strict regular sleep-wake schedule
Treatment of co-occurring depression or other conditions
self_help_that_supports_care: Keeping a sleep diary for two weeks before the appointment
Planning short naps rather than fighting through
Alarms, light, and a routine for the hard morning window
Not driving when sleepy, and talking to a doctor about driving rules

when_to_reach_out: If you sleep well but still can't stay awake by day for months, ask a doctor for a referral to a sleep clinic. Do not drive if you feel sleepy; tell your doctor so the risk can be managed.
is_not: Being tired because of not enough sleep, shift work, medication, or a medical illness isn't hypersomnolence disorder. Sleep apnoea and narcolepsy cause daytime sleepiness too and need their own tests.
hope_note: With a diagnosis and the right treatment, people with hypersomnolence get their days back.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.

in_young_people: Hypersomnolence often starts in the late teens, when it's easily blamed on 'teenage sleep'. A sleep diary and a sleep study tell the difference.
